title: Man. Post. Cap. VIII: first — tree interdict syllogism; conclusion conceded
pass_a_gloss: The first breaks out from the interdict of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil: if that ban and threat looked not only to the first parents but to the whole human race, then the breach of that command made not only them but the whole race liable to death—and the prior is true, so the latter. The major's first part (about the interdict) is outside controversy: who denies the Lord gave the law not only to Adam but to all posterity, or that by that law all were forbidden that fruit? The consequence shows in the event: when the ban was broken, Adam and all posterity became liable to death. Placeus first concedes the conclusion—it fits his view as well as his opponent's: he firmly believes with him that Adam's transgression made the whole race liable to death. The question between them is only the mode.
pass_b_english: The first breaks out from the interdict of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, and proceeds thus. If that interdict, you say, and the threat looked not only to the first parents but also to the whole human race, it follows that the transgression of that Command made not only the first parents liable to death, but also the whole human race. But the prior is true. Therefore the latter also. The first part of the major (which concerns the interdict) is outside controversy: for who will deny that the Lord gave the law not only to Adam but also to all posterity? Who will deny that by that law eating of that fruit was forbidden to all men? And the consequence is manifest from the event: for when the interdict was violated, both Adam and all posterity were made liable to death. At the outset I concede the conclusion of this argument of yours: for it is friendly to my opinion as well as to yours. I believe firmly with you that Adam's transgression made not only the first parents liable to death, but also the whole human race. But the question between us is only about the mode by which that transgression made the whole human race liable to death.
source_text: Primum erumpit ex interdicto arboris scientiae boni & mali, & sic procedit. Si interdictum illud, inquis, & comminatio non tantum primos parentes spectavit, sed etiam totum genus humanum, sequitur transgressionem illius Mandati non tantum primos parentes morti obnoxios fecisse, sed etiam totum genus humanum. Atqui verum prius. Ergo & posterius. Prima pars maioris (quae est de interdicto) extra controversiam est: nam quis inficias ibit Dominum legem dedisse non tantum Adamo, sed etiam posteris omnibus? quis negabit lege illa interdictum omnibus hominibus esum illius fructus? Consequentia vero manifesta est ex eventu: Nam violato interdicto, & Adam & omnes posteri morti obnoxii facti sunt. Principio huius tui argumenti conclusionem concedo: est enim tam meae quam tuae sententiae amica. Credo tecum firmiter, transgressionem Adami non tantum primos parentes morti obnoxios fecisse, sed etiam totum genus humanum. Sed quaestio est inter nos duntaxat de modo, quo transgressio illa totum genus humanum morti obnoxium fecit.
